title: Klein tunneling through an asymmetric barrier: Symmetric transmission and directional pair creation
authors: Andre G. Campos, Denys I. Bondar
abstract: We prove that the transmission probability for the Klein tunneling through a spatially asymmetric barrier is the same for left and right incidence whenever each asymptotic lead carries a single propagating channel per direction. Time-dependent Wigner-function simulations confirm this and locate the missing directionality in the barrier's interior, where a sharp edge generates several times more under-barrier negative-energy population than a smooth one. Directional control in the Klein regime therefore resides in pair production rather than in the transmitted current.
summary: This paper proves that the transmission probability for Klein tunneling through an asymmetric barrier is symmetric. However, using time-dependent simulations, the authors show this asymmetry is not in the transmitted current but rather in the generation of negative-energy states within the barrier region. Therefore, directional control in this regime must be sought by analyzing pair production rather than just particle flux.
main_problem: The study investigates whether Klein tunneling through a spatially asymmetric potential barrier maintains left-right symmetry for Dirac fermions, contrasting with expectations of asymmetry.
main_result: Transmission probability remains symmetric ($T_L = T_R$), but the asymmetry manifests in the interior dynamics as a directionally dependent population of negative-energy states (pair creation).
method: The analysis combines time-independent scattering matrix arguments with time-dependent Wigner-function simulations in phase space.
model_or_system: The system is modeled by the relativistic Dirac equation describing quantum particle scattering off a one-dimensional, spatially asymmetric potential barrier $M(x)$.
key_observables: Transmission probability ($T$), Reflection probability ($R$), and the population of under-barrier negative-energy states.
important_parameters: The analysis is restricted to asymptotic leads carrying exactly one propagating channel per direction.
main_assumptions: The stationary state analysis assumes current conservation, while the time-dependent part relies on Wigner function propagation in phase space.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the tunneling probability, reflection probability, and negative energy population for both left and right incidence across an asymmetric barrier, comparing sharp vs. smooth edges.
paper_structure: The paper first uses time-independent scattering theory to prove $T_L = T_R$. It then employs time-dependent Wigner-function simulations to locate the source of asymmetry in the interior negative-energy population, concluding that pair production, not current, carries the directional information.
why_interesting: The finding that asymptotic transport is robust while internal dynamics are sensitive provides a nuanced view of how symmetry breaking can be 'hidden' from simple current measurements, which is relevant for understanding non-equilibrium quantum transport in mesoscopic systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The spatially asymmetric barrier V (x) used in the simulations, in natural units. One edge is sharp and the other decays over an extended smooth tail, while the asymptotic values on the two sides coincide, V (x →−∞) = V (x → +∞) = 0. The barrier height exceeds the rest energy mc2 = 1, so the dynamics lies in the Klein regime. The dashed lines at x = ±12 delimit the interior region; |x| > 12 defines the reflected and transmitted populations quoted in the text.

FIG. 2. Time-resolved observables for the two propagations, one in which the wave packet meets the sharp edge of the barrier of Fig. 1 first and one in which it meets the smooth edge first. (a) Tunneling probability, i.e., the population be- yond the barrier. The two curves coincide, confirming Theo- rem 1 (b) Reflection probability, i.e., the population in front of the barrier. The two curves separate. (c) Population of the negative-energy states. The sharp edge generates about four times more antiparticles than the smooth edge; this popula- tion remains under the barrier and accounts for the difference in panel (b).

Fig. 3(a), is a single compact positive Gaussian displaced toward the barrier along the momentum axis. The barrier of Fig. 1 is held fixed throughout; the two propagations differ only in where the initial packet is pre- pared and in which direction it is launched, so that it en- counters the sharp edge first in one run and the smooth edge first in the other. In the first run the packet starts to the left of the barrier and moves toward +x: we then call the probability of finding the particle at x < −12 the reflection probability and the probability of finding it at x > 12 the tunneling probability (see Fig. 2). FIG. 3. Phase-space portrait of the two propagations, dis- played as the Wigner function W(x, p) in natural units. (a) Initial state, in the geometry in which it faces the smooth edge. (b) Final state of that run. (c) Final state of the run facing the sharp edge, plotted after the phase-space inversion W(x, p) →W(−x, −p), which maps the mirrored geometry onto the axes of panel (b) and allows the two final states to be compared directly. The dashed lines at x = ±12 delimit the interior region entering Fig. 2. The sharp edge generates a rich interference pattern, the phase-space signature of zit- terbewegung, concentrated underneath the barrier.
